one_liner: This paper shows that the order of elements in sets matters for sequence-to-sequence models and proposes methods to handle unordered inputs and outputs by searching over permutations during training.
paragraphs: Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have revolutionized tasks like machine translation and image captioning by using the chain rule to model sequences. However, many real-world problems involve inputs or outputs that are unordered sets—such as sorting a set of numbers or generating a list of detected objects in an image—where no natural ordering exists. The paper questions whether the arbitrary order we impose on such data affects model performance and argues that since seq2seq models are sensitive to input/output order, choosing the right ordering can significantly impact learning efficiency and accuracy.

To address this, the authors extend seq2seq to handle sets by introducing two key innovations: (1) For input sets, they propose encoding elements in different orders during training to expose the model to various permutations; (2) For output sets, they introduce a novel loss function that searches over possible output orders during training to find the one that minimizes prediction error, effectively treating order as a latent variable. This allows the model to learn which ordering is most useful without assuming any predefined structure.

Experiments on artificial tasks like sorting numbers and estimating joint probabilities of graphical models, as well as real-world tasks like language modeling and parsing, demonstrate that carefully choosing or learning the order of elements improves performance significantly. The results show that even when no natural order exists, some orders lead to better convergence and accuracy—proving that 'order matters.' The proposed methods enable seq2seq models to generalize beyond sequences and handle set-based tasks robustly, opening new avenues for modeling structured outputs without hand-crafted structures.
key_takeaways: The order of elements in sets significantly impacts seq2seq model performance, even when no natural ordering exists.
A new loss function that searches over possible output orders during training enables seq2seq models to learn optimal permutations for set outputs.
Input sets can be effectively encoded by training on multiple random orderings, making seq2seq models robust to unordered inputs.
This work extends seq2seq beyond sequences, allowing it to handle set-based tasks like sorting and probabilistic modeling without requiring tree or graph structures.
The approach is general-purpose, applicable to both artificial and real-world tasks, and demonstrates that latent ordering can be learned from data.
eli5: Imagine you have a box of mixed-up toys, and you need to line them up in the right order. Even though the toys don’t come with instructions on how to arrange them, trying different orders helps you find the best way to sort them. This paper teaches computers to try many different ways of lining up things that don’t have a fixed order, and then pick the best one to get the right answer.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of sequence-to-sequence models and RNNs/LSTMs
Familiarity with probability chains and conditional likelihoods
applications: Sorting unordered data like numbers or timestamps without assuming a predefined sequence
Generating lists of detected objects in images where order doesn't matter (e.g., object detection outputs)
title: Order Matters: Seq2Seq for Sets
